text: A young man kills his best friend in a street fight, and then has to go on living where both of them were known. The civil strife in Shantham is not scenery the camera pans across; it is the reason two friends stood on opposite sides of a road, and Jayaraj leaves Velayudhan no clean exit, since the other side is political and plans its answer at leisure. Ninety-five minutes, Malayalam, 1999. At that scale guilt stops being interior weather and becomes a question of which house to enter, whose eye to meet, which road home is still available. India's national award for best feature went to it. What the film holds onto is the interval between the thing done and the reckoning being arranged for it, and how ordinary a man's days stay while he waits inside it.

Fuyukichi Takano taught at a university, then took a job at a museum, and now loses that too because his memory will not hold. Shunya Ito gives the household 125 minutes, which is long for a story with no incident larger than a misplaced afternoon, and the length is the argument: an illness like this is not an event but a timetable. Who sits with him. Who repeats the same sentence without sighing. The direction of travel is what surprises — the diagnosis does not seal the old man away from his family, it presses them into daily contact, and the film attends to the awkward practical warmth that follows rather than to decline. Japan sent it to the Academy Awards for 1985. Its care goes into the arithmetic of a household reorganising itself around one person who can no longer be left alone.

Comedy is an odd instrument for loneliness, and this Taiwanese picture from 1984 picks it up anyway. Lao Mo is a veteran with his working life behind him who has decided he will not spend what remains of it by himself, and Li Youning stages that decision as a series of arrangements rather than a romance — introductions, terms, money, the involvement of people whose interests are not his. The comedy runs on how little margin he has; remove the margin and the same scenes would be unbearable. It took the Golden Horse for best feature. At 114 minutes the film keeps its nerve by staying at the level of negotiation, where an old man's wish for company is not a sentiment to be honoured but a proposal that other people have to weigh.

September 1940, and a broke forty-nine-year-old arrives in Vichy carrying copies of a manifesto he had to publish himself. Henri Marre wants a place in the new administration and believes it is owed to him; his case is method, since he is an engineer and efficiency is the virtue he trusts, and a defeated France will need men who can make things run. Emmanuel Marre takes 155 minutes over the small competences by which a man makes himself useful to an authoritarian regime, and puts the comedy exactly where it belongs, in the distance between the manifesto's language and the errands. The screenplay is what the film was recognised for, and it earns that: nothing Henri says about his patriotism is a lie he tells others before he tells himself.

She is a voice on the radio before she is a person in a room, and the order matters. Lee Hsing's young man has nothing but time and no idea what to do with it; the broadcaster he stumbles across has a shift, a microphone and a script that has to be finished by a particular hour, and what separates them is not class or character so much as whether a day has a shape. Taipei in 1979 gets its due — streets, work, the distance a city can put between two people who might easily never meet twice. The Golden Horse for best feature went to it. At 102 minutes the comedy stays mild, and the subject underneath it is stranger: a voice sent out to nobody in particular, and one listener who starts arranging his week around when it comes on.

Seventy-two minutes is very little time for what this film takes on. Goutam Ghose follows a woman out of a nomadic community of crow hunters in Andhra Pradesh, across the country to south Bengal, where she keeps herself alive by occult practice among people who are not hers. The landlord who exploits her is not a villain of temperament but of position, which is harder to film and more useful to see. At that length there is no room for backstory or for explanations of custom; the situation is underway before the audience arrives, and the Bengal around her runs on arrangements she had no part in making. India's national award for best feature went to it in 1980. Everything the film has to say sits in the gap between what this woman can do and what she is allowed to hold.

A wealthy widow and a girl described as frivolous, and ninety minutes given over to what passes between them. Debaki Bose made it in 1957 under the title Sagar Sangamey, and the pairing is the entire design: one woman with means and standing and the obligations attached to both, one with neither and no evident wish to acquire them. The film keeps its attention on the two of them rather than on some man placed between them to explain the attachment. It took the national award for the year's best Bengali feature. What the premise promises is friction of manner rather than plot — a settled routine meeting a temperament that will not keep time with it, and an older woman discovering that her authority is worth nothing in the one attachment she has come to want.

Being found innocent is where the damage starts, not where it ends. Matthias is picked up for something small, processed, released with his name cleared and nothing else repaired, and Norbert Kückelmann spends the ninety-eight minutes on the processing rather than the offence: the waiting, the forms, the officials for whom he is one file among many. The film declines to make him sympathetic first. He was already a misfit, already short of what was expected of him, and the machinery meets him at his least defensible, which is exactly where most stories look away. What this 1973 German drama studies is not injustice in the legal sense, since the verdict goes his way, but the ordinary indifference of people doing their jobs correctly, and what it costs a man with nothing in reserve.

A thousand nights on a bed of stones was the title of the story Khwaja Ahmad Abbas wrote first. The film he made from it in 1962 stays exactly where that phrase puts it, on the pavement. The people sleeping there are not a backdrop to an argument about industrial growth; they are what the growth is made of, and Abbas declines to arrange the two facts into a triumph with a sad margin beside it. Two hours leaves room for the logistics — where belongings go, what a household is with no walls to define it, how a night is got through and a morning begun. It took India's national award for best feature. The steadiness comes from treating the pavement dwellers as people with business to attend to rather than as an illustration of a condition.

Nadira's marriage is fixed on the day she first bleeds, and the person she tells is a childhood friend. K. P. Suveeran built the film around the Byari community — its language, its customs, and above all its rules on marriage and divorce, which are not background here but the machinery the story runs on. Her husband is three times her age and devoted to her, and that is the most useful complication in it: what presses on this household is not one man's cruelty and could not be fixed by finding a kinder one. India's national award for best feature went to it. A hundred minutes, made in 2010, held to domestic scale throughout — rooms, meals, a child, a life conducted on terms other people settled — and addressed, finally, to the people who write the rules.

Taiwan's best-feature prize for 1970 went to a family drama, and that is the firmest thing anyone can hold about Pai Ching-jui's picture now. Family and Drama are the only genres attached to it; 108 minutes is the only measurement; the language is Mandarin. Those still say something. A film built to that description has to hold an audience with people who cannot walk out on one another, with the arithmetic of a household, with rooms rather than landscapes. And a jury calling such a work the year's best is making a claim about where the pressures of that moment were being felt — indoors, among relatives, at the scale where money and distance register first. Anyone who turns up a copy is looking straight at that claim.

The offer is straightforward: money to anyone who can produce a ghost. Surendra was exiled from his village as a young man, made his life in the city, and comes back to news that a phantom killed his father, so he posts a prize on the reasonable assumption that nobody can collect it. Biplab Roy Chowdhury's film comes labelled as horror, and the label is exact, though not in the usual way, because the dread is in the transaction. The village has belief and no money. The visitor has money and no belief. India's national award for best feature went to it in 1978. Om Puri plays the man who thinks he is administering reason, and what the film watches is how fast a hungry place will supply whatever a rich visitor says he wants.

Everyone wants to stop General Tsai from leaving Peking, and that single vector holds up a whole film. Eighty-eight minutes of action, built on a structure that either sustains itself or falls apart in the first reel: a man trying to get out of a city, and a city organised against it. Peter Yang Kwan took the Golden Horse for best feature with it in 1972. Movement is the argument — every scene has to answer whether the general is nearer the gate or further from it, and everything else, allegiance, motive, who owes what to whom, must be delivered while he keeps moving. Pictures that carry their meaning in geography rather than dialogue tend to survive their decade, because a chase does not date the way a speech does.

An Indian production of 1960 built a Bengali feature around a Scots-Irish woman, and gave her 156 minutes. Bijoy Bose's subject is Sister Nivedita — teacher, writer, social worker, disciple of Swami Vivekananda — whose life moved through classrooms, households and public argument rather than through incident, which makes the length a requirement rather than an indulgence. The pressure such a film has to locate is the one on her foreignness: she arrives already convinced, and everything after that is carried out among people entitled to ask what brought her. India's national award for best feature went to it. The hard problem here is one biographies rarely admit to — how to dramatise a conviction that was settled before the first scene.
